Our findings show that current watermarking methods can be reliably defeated under realistic attack conditions, highlighting the need for fundamentally different watermarking designs that decouple detection scores from token probability shifts.

title: Secure Multimodal Federated Optimization via Hierarchical DNA-Based Key Management
summary: Federated optimization over heterogeneous multimodal data enables distributed institutions to collaboratively optimize a shared model using medical images, genomic profiles, clinical records, and physiological signals without centralizing raw data. However, protecting modality-specific data throughout the optimization lifecycle remains insufficiently explored, particularly when heterogeneous modalities require separate encryption keys and selective local access. This paper proposes a secure multimodal federated optimization framework that separates local data protection from federated-update protection. A trusted key-management authority securely provisions one client key through Hybrid Public Key Encryption (HPKE), from which each client locally derives modality-specific symmetric keys using the domain-separated HMAC-based Extract-and-Expand Key Derivation Function (HKDF). Heterogeneous modalities are mapped into a unified DNA-domain representation and processed through a DNA-origami-inspired structural transformation before authenticated encryption with AES-GCM. During local optimization, only the required modalities are decrypted within an authorized client environment. Individual model updates are independently protected through secure aggregation, allowing the coordinator to observe only aggregated updates rather than each client's contribution. Together, these components establish a structured approach to modality-specific protection and secure collaborative optimization, integrating hierarchical key management, authenticated local encryption, and aggregation-level update protection within a unified framework.

title: Local Allow, Global Deny: Why Per-Action Authorization Does Not Compose in LLM Agents
summary: Autonomous LLM agents act through tools under per-action authorization: a local guard screens each tool call in isolation. We show that local authorization does not compose into global authorization. A compositional authorization failure (CAF) is a locally authorized execution, or a pair of locally authorized executions, that violates a global policy spanning intent, purpose, provenance, consent, and delegation. We characterize CAFs along two axes, expressiveness (single-trace safety versus relational k-safety) and observability (a ladder of monitor profiles). Our central result is an impossibility: relational purpose violations form a 2-safety hyperproperty with no per-trace locus of blame, so a per-action monitor that never raises a false alarm detects none of them, independent of the underlying model or decision procedure; they become visible only under cross-execution monitoring, which none of the six guardrails we survey implements. We make this constructive with AL-SYNTH, a SAT/SMT synthesizer (using no language model) that emits minimal CAF witnesses, each checked against an exhaustive oracle. The empirical signature is sharp: across nine LLM judges the per-action view approves the synthesized witness almost without exception, blocking it at a rate comparable to a benign control, yet the same models flag it when shown the two executions together. Per-action authorization is therefore structurally insufficient for relational policy conjuncts not reducible to single-trace safety: to bound them, a monitor must compare executions or accept false alarms.

title: DISTA-LP: Privacy-Preserving Distributed Linear Programming for Metric Differential Privacy
summary: Linear-programming (LP) mechanisms for metric differential privacy (mDP) enable fine-grained, task-aware utility control, but they are computationally expensive and become privacy-fragile in distributed settings: uploading user-specific LP coefficient matrices (e.g., distance and loss blocks) to a central solver can itself leak sensitive information. We present DISTA-LP, a privacy-preserving distributed mDP optimization framework that replaces raw coefficient uploads with compact surrogate parameterizations and releases only calibrated, perturbed parameter vectors, thereby reducing both upload-stage leakage and problem dimensionality. On the server side, DISTA-LP reconstructs approximate coefficients and solves a scalable mastersubproblem formulation via Benders decomposition. To certify end-to-end privacy, we introduce a probabilistic mDP (PmDP) auditor that empirically quantifies the privacy loss induced by parameter release, allocates the required privacy budget prior to optimization, and composes it with the downstream mechanism to obtain an end-to-end mDP guarantee. Experiments on large realworld road-network datasets (Rome, New York City, and London) show that DISTA-LP achieves near-zero mDP violation rates, substantially reduces computation time compared to monolithic and hybrid baselines, and matches or improves utility, thereby demonstrating stronger upload privacy and significantly improved scalability.

title: Big Secrets Small Shares: Revisiting Secure Multi-Party Computation
summary: At CRYPTO 2007, Damgård and Nielsen introduced a preprocessing approach to multi-party computation (MPC) to achieve linear communication complexity. Another approach to reduce communication complexity was proposed by Cramer, Damgård, and de Haan at EUROCRYPT 2007, which involved using ramp-secret sharing schemes to jointly share base-field components of secrets from the extension field. In this paper, we combine these two ideas to achieve a non-asymptotic reduction of communication cost in a multi-phase MPC setup. We introduce a new modification of the ramp secret sharing scheme, called compact sharing, and tailor the MPC protocol to accommodate this modification. Compact sharing masks the polynomial coefficients that would otherwise leak during degree reduction. The protocol provides perfect security against static semi-honest adversaries under an explicit tradeoff between the corruption threshold and the extension degree. When the extension degree scales linearly with the number of parties, the gate-evaluation core achieves constant communication overhead relative to an extension-field element, amortized over full preprocessing batches; input and output communication is counted separately.

title: Bridging Digital Deception and Physical Fidelity: A Spatio-Temporal Attack on Cognitive Radars
summary: As cognitive radars evolve towards the end-to-end processing of one-dimensional complex baseband sequences, deep networks face severe adversarial threats. However, existing attacks encounter dual limitations in practical electronic warfare: low cross-architecture transferability and severe vulnerability to physical channel distortions, which degrades their tactical reliability. To overcome these bottlenecks, we propose a physical prior-driven Segmented Spatio-Temporal Attack (SSTA). First, a global-local feature decoupling segmentation mechanism interrupts the adversarial gradients' dependence on long-range sequence coherence, bridging the cross-architecture feature gap. Second, moving beyond static norm constraints devoid of physical semantics, we abstract channel distortions into differentiable spatio-temporal operators, integrating them into momentum iterations via an Expectation over Transformation (EoT) strategy. Comprehensive cross-evaluations across 9 heterogeneous models spanning CNNs, RNNs, and Transformers demonstrate that SSTA outperforms the state-of-the-art baseline by 10.36% in Average Black-Box Attack Success Rate. Furthermore, baseband equivalent simulations confirm that the generated waveforms survive extreme physical distortions and, after matched filtering, achieve zero main-lobe attenuation (0 dB) with noise floor lift strictly within Constant False Alarm Rate tolerances. SSTA successfully unifies digital-domain deception and physical-domain fidelity, providing crucial support for CEW security assessment.

title: The Show-Up Attack: When Subagents Win Over Their Supervisor
summary: Multi-agent systems are increasingly deployed to coordinate multiple large language model (LLM) agents. However, this also creates new attack surfaces: malicious agents may have chances to exploit the coordination. In this paper, we propose and study the \textit{show-up attack}, in which a malicious subagent manipulates the supervisor into involving it in tasks beyond its assigned scope. To evaluate this risk, we propose SUA-Arena, which implements 6 attack strategies and contains 188 test cases. Then, we evaluate 6 frontier LLMs and find that all of them are vulnerable to show-up attacks. For example, GPT-5.6-Sol as a supervisor suffers an ASR of up to 0.93. Mitigation strategies such as prompting and restricted communication fail to reduce the risk consistently. These results show that multi-agent systems need explicit mechanisms for enforcing authority boundaries.

title: When EVM Defaults Break: Three SDK Patterns for UTXO-Family Wallets
summary: Mainstream Web3 SDKs (e.g., ethers.js, viem) bundle three coupled assumptions: an account-based ledger, a single secp256k1 signer, and input-selection-free transaction construction. These assumptions fail once a chain adopts an extended-UTXO model (here, the Cell model on Nervos CKB), and once the wallet population spans heterogeneous cryptographic primitives (secp256k1, WebAuthn, Schnorr). Using CKBers' Codebase (CCC), a TypeScript SDK, this retrospective case study extracts three recurring patterns from release history and exported APIs: a Transaction Composer that makes capacity-aware input completion and fee estimation declarative, a Unified Signer Abstraction that normalizes signing across heterogeneous wallets behind one interface, and a Connector UI component that ships per-wallet onboarding as a drop-in. The contribution is the articulation of these patterns as transferable design lessons for SDKs targeting UTXO-family ledgers and heterogeneous wallet populations.

title: Act on Your Behalf, Beyond Your Authorization: Benchmarking LLM Agent Authorization Alignment
summary: When an LLM agent acts on behalf of a user, it is expected to act within the authorization scope the user grants. Existing agent evaluations largely measure task completion or harmful consequences and can therefore overlook actions that violate this delegation without producing conventional safety or privacy harms. We introduce AuthorizationBench, a benchmark of authorization alignment grounded in documented real-world cases. A scalable construction pipeline produces 286 executable tasks spanning situational triggers, the presence or absence of direct harmful consequences, and ten application domains. We execute every task with four models at two reasoning-effort settings across three agent harnesses in an authorization-aware sandbox that keeps authorized and out-of-authorization paths executable and observable, yielding 6,864 trajectories. Agents act out of authorization in 19.2% of trajectories, with rates ranging from 10.5% to 26.6% across the 24 configurations. Task completion does not imply authorization. Increasing reasoning effort leaves the aggregate rate nearly unchanged, with effects varying across models. On controlled pairs, agents act out of authorization at similar rates with (17.9%) and without (20.8%) direct harmful consequences, and more often under benign pressures than malicious injections (23.5% versus 17.6%, p=0.002). Our results show that task capability, additional reasoning, and consequence-oriented safety evaluation do not by themselves ensure authorization alignment. Moreover, agents that consult the principal before completing a task exhibit lower rates of out-of-authorization behavior (14.0% versus 21.6%, p<0.001), pointing to a tension between agent autonomy and preserving users' decision authority that calls for further human-centered study. Dataset and code are available at https://github.com/PEACH-Research-Lab/AuthorizationBench .

title: KNOX: Hardware-assisted Regulatory Sandbox for Generative Models
summary:
Regulations require companies to run AI models in a regulatory sandbox, an isolated environment that enables monitoring model behavior by regulators, prior to deployment. But, they do not spell out the technical mechanisms to design such a sandbox. Ideally, a regulatory sandbox should show (i) compliance (checks against regulations, and deviations from intended behavior, i.e., unauthorized tool and system calls); (ii) confidentiality (protects model weights from regulators); (iii) attestability (produces tamper-resistant evidence of model behavior for monitoring); and (iv) scalability (evidence is verifiable by multiple regulators). Several prior works (information-flow control, prompt-injection defenses, control-flow integrity, and traditional sandboxing) address specific compliance aspects but lack confidentiality, attestability, and scalability. TEEs meet some of these requirements, but simply running models inside a TEE is insufficient as we need compliance mechanisms.
  We present KNOX, the first regulatory sandbox, built by running AI workloads inside TEEs. We demonstrate KNOX using agentic workloads. For compliance, we derive an attested policy manifest (with the applicable regulations, the expected tool calls, and the permitted system calls) for a given user prompt. Before an executor performs an action, an attested reference monitor compares it against the attested policy manifest and allows it only if it matches. Every action and verdict is recorded in an attested execution graph, enabling regulators to verify the model's execution and its compliance. We show that KNOX meets all requirements, and can check for compliance with regulations and deviations from intended behavior (e.g., due to prompt injection); and incurs low overhead (<1%).

title: Adversarial Benchmarks and BenchDoor Attacks: Exploiting Benchmark Incentives for Backdoor Attacks
summary: Machine learning benchmarks act as guideposts for model development and spur the creation of training datasets intended to improve benchmark scores. We introduce BenchDoor, a family of data poisoning attacks that exploits this incentive. Beyond preserving benign performance, BenchDoor requires benchmark gains that encourage adoption of data that also implants a backdoor. The adversary either manipulates a benchmark's training or test data, creating an adversarial benchmark, or supplies an independent training dataset while leaving the benchmark unchanged. We formalize five attack scenarios, including training on rewritten test examples and applying similarity-based decontamination. Across multiple-choice Q&A, text classification, and open-ended Q&A with Qwen and Gemma models, BenchDoor achieves positive benchmark gains for all 30 evaluated configurations, with held-out attack success rates of 82.33% to 100.00% at poisoning rates of 2% to 10%. Both objectives remain achievable after synthetic data generation and similarity-based decontamination, with attack success rates of at least 90.33%. These findings show how benchmarks can serve as attack vectors both through their own data and through training resources that deliver improvements on them.

title: Beyond the Prompt: Recovering Hidden Concepts in Text-to-Image Models
summary: Text-to-image models can generate visual concepts that their prompts never mention, and recent work shows that such associations can be implanted so that ordinary prompts trigger them. Auditing this behavior requires recovering the description that a prompt omits. Existing prompt optimizers are not well suited to this task. Gradient-based methods require backward access to the scoring encoder. Discrete evolutionary search treats semantically unrelated tokens as equally close. Language-model-guided search requires one inference call per candidate, which limits exploration. This paper presents EmbGA, an embedding-space genetic algorithm that recovers concepts present in a set of images but absent from the prompt that generated them. EmbGA keeps the population structure of genetic search but applies its operators in the token embedding space. Crossover interpolates between parent embeddings, and mutation moves an embedding toward a randomly drawn vocabulary embedding. Each offspring is then projected back to discrete tokens before scoring, so every evaluated candidate is a valid token sequence. We evaluate EmbGA on two benchmarks against six optimizers under two exploration budgets. EmbGA achieves the highest alignment when the exploration budget is large, recovers the most grounded tokens on natural images, and runs much faster than language-model-guided search.

title: Privacy-Preserving Personalized Federated Learning (PPP-FL) for Medical Imaging
summary: Federated learning (FL) is a distributed machine learning paradigm that reduces transmission costs, mitigates cross-border data sharing restrictions, and enhances privacy by keeping raw data on local devices. Clients in FL systems train local models and share only updates, which are aggregated by a central server. While this setup limits direct data exposure, FL remains vulnerable to privacy attacks. Existing attack and defense strategies have largely been developed for centralized systems, and adapting them to FL introduces new challenges due to its unique architecture and training workflow. In this work, we first propose a model inversion attack on FL systems using Deep Convolutional Generative Adversarial Networks (DCGANs) in the context of large-scale medical imaging. Our method operates under realistic assumptions about the attacker's knowledge and capabilities. We then examine the effect of client-side differential privacy (DP) in mitigating privacy leakage and incorporate personalized FL to improve model performance under DP settings. Experiments on the Brain MRI ND-5 dataset show that DCGAN-based attacks can reconstruct semantically meaningful synthetic images, revealing significant risks to the privacy of training data. Applying DP reduces attack success but introduces an accuracy trade-off, which is further overcome by personalized FL at each client side. We also evaluate how different aggregation algorithms affect both attack vulnerability and defense effectiveness, underscoring the critical role of aggregation strategies. The proposed attack-and-defense framework is model-agnostic and applicable to a wide range of FL-based systems.

title: NetGuise: Adversarial Traffic Generation for Early-Stage Classifier Evasion
summary:
Early-stage encrypted traffic classifiers make decisions from only the first few packets of a connection, enabling low-latency classification but raising robustness concerns under realistic traffic morphing. Existing adversarial traffic generation methods often assume complete flows, feature-level perturbations, or iterative runtime feedback, which do not match the constraints of early-stage execution.
  We present NetGuise, a target-conditioned traffic morphing framework that generates packet-level padding and non-negative delay actions while preserving packet direction, ordering, and packet count and respecting MTU, bandwidth, and latency constraints. We evaluate NetGuise for censorship evasion under two observation interfaces, i) a history-only causal interface for online packet-by-packet execution, ii) and a full-window oracle interface that provides an upper-bound characterization of early-stage morphability. On VANT, NetGuise achieves 33.2% mean targeted evasion under the causal interface versus 82.0% under the oracle interface; on UTMobileNet, the corresponding results are 5.6% and 81.8%. NetGuise outperforms the strongest causal baseline, BAP, on both datasets and, on VANT, reduces bandwidth overhead from 19.80% to 3.02% and generation latency from 37.42 ms/flow to 1.16 ms/flow. Under the oracle interface, it achieves up to 85.7% targeted evasion, retains 43.5% after four rounds of adaptive censor retraining, and maintains 48% under zero-shot cross-environment transfer. Our results show that early-stage classifiers can remain morphable despite high clean accuracy and that robustness evaluation should account for targeted morphability, observation constraints, defender adaptation, and operational network conditions.

title: SRE: Accelerating Zero-Knowledge Proofs via Scalar Redundancy Elimination in Multi-Scalar Multiplication
summary: Multi-Scalar Multiplication (MSM) is a fundamental cryptographic operation used in Elliptic Curve Cryptography (ECC) across a wide range of applications. Its computation involves intensive elliptic curve point additions (PADD). MSM plays a critical role in cryptographic primitives such as polynomial commitments and zero-knowledge proofs (ZKPs), where it often becomes the runtime bottleneck. Consequently, optimizing MSM is an active area of research focused on reducing computational complexity and accelerating performance. The current state-of-the-art algorithm for large-scale MSM is Pippenger's bucket method, which consists of three main steps: point merging, bucket aggregation, and window aggregation. Among these, the point merging step is the primary performance bottleneck. Our work targets this major computational bottleneck. To reduce operations for practical applications, we propose a novel Scalar Redundancy Elimination (SRE) algorithm with three approaches: a vanilla array-based approach, a list-based greedy approach, and a list-based exhaustive approach, all incorporating an early stopping technique. Depending on the use case, these strategies can be integrated into our modified MSM algorithm, which is based on Pippenger's bucket method. As a result, our proposed MSM algorithm, enhanced with the SRE technique, incurs less than $3\%$ additional search time, while reducing the number of operations by $25\%$, leading to a $30\%$ speedup in runtime compared to the standard Pippenger's bucket method. This translates to a $10 \sim 20\%$ runtime reduction in various ZKP systems that rely heavily on MSM.

title: Privacy-Preserving Robustness-Guided Testing
summary: In industries like semi-conductors and aerospace, it is common for the design company to contract out part of the testing process to a Testing-as-a-Service (TaaS) company. In such a setup, both parties want to keep their intellectual property private (i.e. unknown to the other party): namely the design and its output traces for the designer, and the detailed correctness specifications for the tester. We demonstrate a practical way for conducting provably private TaaS using a cryptographically secure multi-party computation protocol. We do so for the common setup where the specification is in Signal Temporal Logic, and testing is done using robustness-guided falsification. Our implementation carefully separates the steps of falsification, and manages to be $\textit{maximally secure}$, in the sense that the parties learn the absolutely minimum necessary for falsification. For up to a 100-dimensional input search space, the generation of one test takes less than 80 msec, and the overhead of the privacy-preserving protocol is less than 6x. These numbers mean that privacy-preserving TaaS is practical, thus enabling TaaS in security-sensitive industries.

title: Interflow: Breaking the Offline-Online Barrier for Private AI at the Edge
summary: Privacy-preserving machine learning (PPML) offers a promising path toward bringing powerful AI services to the edge without exposing sensitive user data. However, its practical deployment remains constrained by the high communication, computation, and data-movement costs of secure multi-party computation (MPC), particularly during nonlinear inference. Existing MPC systems typically decouple input-independent correlated randomness generation from online execution, creating substantial memory pressure to buffer single-use cryptographic data. Moreover, limited storage can force a stop-and-refill execution pattern that repeatedly stalls the pipeline to replenish these buffers, bringing randomness generation back onto the critical path. We propose Interflow, an algorithm-hardware co-design that rethinks this separation by batch-wise processing and pipelining correlated-randomness generation with online execution: while the current batch consumes pre-generated randomness to execute secure nonlinear operations, correlation generation proceeds concurrently for the next batch. By leveraging interleaved execution, efficient data movement, and hardware acceleration, the design transforms preprocessing from a serialized, storage-intensive offline phase into a continuously overlapped pipeline that generates correlated randomness closer to the point of consumption, reducing memory footprint and data movement overhead. Implemented on the Zynq UltraScale+ ZCU102, Interflow improves nonlinear evaluation throughput by up to 1.55x for CNN operators and 1.48x for transformer operators. It achieves up to 1.26x speedup for ResNet-50 and up to 1.21x speedup for BERT-base, and reduces memory footprint by up to 37%, compared with baseline frameworks.

title: AgenticVulHunter: Bringing Local Agentic Vulnerability Hunting to Your Terminal
summary: Finding vulnerabilities early, before they can affect the production system, is important for reducing the risk of any software attacks. However, detecting vulnerabilities during secure code review is still difficult because the vulnerable code logic may depend on lines found across different repository files. Recent approaches such as AgenticSCR have shown that LLM agents can explore repository files and use security knowledge to improve secure code review. However, these approaches mainly rely on external commercial LLMs and can provide a large amount of security knowledge to the agent at once. This creates an important question of whether agentic secure code review can also be performed effectively using locally deployed open-weight LLMs with more focused and relevant security knowledge. In this paper, we propose AgenticVulHunter, an agentic secure code review approach and tool that can run with a locally deployed open-weight LLM. We evaluate AgenticVulHunter on 144 vulnerability cases from SCRBench using Qwen3-Coder-30B and DeepSeek V3.1 Terminus. We measure what percentage of generated review comments correctly identify the vulnerable location, match the vulnerability type, and provide a relevant security review comment together. AgenticVulHunter achieves an accuracy of 18.4% with Qwen3- Coder-30B and 23.8% with DeepSeek V3.1 Terminus, compared with 11.8% for our AgenticSCR-style reproduction using Qwen3-Coder-30B and 17.5% for AgenticSCR using Claude Sonnet 4.

title: Exposing Vulnerability Monoculture Through Systemic Adversarial Robustness
summary: Beneath the apparent diversity of foundation models lies an increasingly homogeneous technical stack of common training pipelines, distillation methods, and data. These shared algorithmic choices can expose an otherwise distinct model ecosystem to concentrated risks leading to a vulnerability monoculture. Yet current practice in assessing adversarial robustness is restricted to individual robustness scores and attack transfer rates, leaving open the unexplored fundamental question: how many attacks suffice for catastrophic widespread compromise? In this paper, we investigate the empirical nature of shared vulnerabilities within a model pool and introduce Systemic Adversarial Robustness (SAR), a novel measure of shared vulnerability of a model pool through the attack diversity needed to exploit it. Specifically, SAR interpolates between single-attack transferability and independent per-model robustness: small values reveal a vulnerability monoculture, whereas large values indicate that failures are dispersed across models. We theoretically formulate SAR as a partial set-cover problem with provable approximation guarantees---enabling the development of scalable algorithms to empirically measure the systemic adversarial robustness. We empirically test the shared vulnerability of vision and large language models and characterize their shared collective vulnerability curve. Specifically, we demonstrate that model pools distilled from DeepSeek-R1 and Claude Opus 4.6 exhibit lower estimated systemic robustness than their corresponding parent pools, revealing a potential systemic cost of frontier-model distillation. Our framework seeks to establish vulnerability monoculture as a measurable target for a more wholistic adversarial evaluation of model populations.

title: Orchestrating Key Scarcity: Global Capacity Allocation in Hybrid QKD-PQC Networks
summary: This article presents a Distributed Key Management System (DKMS) that provisions quantum-safe symmetric encryption keys to applications across a network. To overcome the distance and rate limitations inherent to Quantum Key Distribution (QKD), the architecture adopts a hybrid design: it utilizes multi-hop trusted relays for physical key transport, while applying an end-to-end Post-Quantum Cryptography (PQC) layer to ensure the relayed key material remains strictly protected from intermediate nodes. Because QKD transforms key generation into a scarce physical resource, managing unpredictable application demands poses a critical capacity allocation problem. The core contribution of this work is an SDN-driven control plane that globally orchestrates the network. Rather than relying on vulnerable hop-by-hop capacity reservations, a central controller simultaneously computes optimal filling rates and multipath routing for all per-peer key buffers. This global orchestration ensures that no application is starved and that all key buffers synchronize their filling processes. Evaluated on a Kubernetes-based digital twin across five distinct network topologies, the controller successfully filled all key buffers to capacity in under six minutes. Furthermore, under deliberately excessive demand, the network demonstrated graceful degradation, safely rejecting excess requests through controlled rate-limiting rather than experiencing catastrophic failure.

title: Detecting AI Training in Datacentre Power
summary: AI governance agreements require methods to detect large model training runs on a monitored computing cluster, without trusting the operator. We develop a method to detect synchronous model training in facility-level power by Viterbi tracking of the wandering iteration cadence. On simulated datacentre power, when the operator makes no attempt to hide, the Viterbi tracker detects at least $96\%$ of training runs against a declared inference workload, at a $1\%$ false-alarm rate and within $0.04$ of the Neyman--Pearson optimum, given a meter that samples at $2$ Hz or faster. Of eight adversarial strategies an operator might use to hide, only extreme variation of the work per iteration evades the tracker. Its strongest form hides training in up to $73\%$ of five-minute observations, but over a day at least $87\%$ of such runs are still caught, at a $0.1\%$ false-alarm rate per run. This adversarial strategy costs no throughput, but in small-scale training the operator needs $93$--$267\%$ more compute to reach the same loss. A modest passive meter is sufficient to make hidden training both detectable and expensive, which makes power metering a promising part of compute verification that does not depend on trusting the operator.

title: Quantum-Seeded Distributed Post-Quantum Group Signatures for 5G V2X Communications
summary: Vehicle-to-Everything (V2X) communications rely on elliptic-curve signatures that a quantum adversary breaks and on pseudonym certificates whose anonymity rests on rotation rate, not cryptography. This work presents qDGSP, a post-quantum V2X infrastructure: a hash-based dynamic group signature scheme (DGSP, over SPHINCS+ and WOTS+) distributed between a central controller and roadside verifiers. Group keys derive deterministically from quantum key distribution (QKD) seeds served over the ETSI GS QKD 014 interface, so no group-signature secret crosses the classical channel. qDGSP-EA (Ephemeral Association) binds an ephemeral ML-DSA-65 key to one group signature per 5G cell: messages remain unlinkable across cells, linkable within one. On a testbed with emulated 5G links, median end-to-end latency stayed within the 100ms ETSI budget for every variant. The qDGSP-EA intra-cell DENM matched the NIST ML-DSA-65 baseline on the wire, and under load EA mode raised delivery from roughly 78% to 93%.

title: Scrambled Multiply-with-Carry Pseudorandom Number Generators
summary: Multiply-with-carry (MWC) generators are very fast pseudorandom number generators whose quality depends on the choice of a multiplier, and is usually assessed by applying the spectral test to an associated multiplicative congruential generator. We show that the special form of the modulus imposes structural limitations on the lattice structure of every MWC generator, which the generalized MWC generators of Goresky and Klapper mitigate; in our tests, xoring each output with its carry removes them. Since these limitations make the usual worst-case criterion useless, we rank candidates by a weighted geometric mean of their figures of merit, which does not depend on their normalization, and suggest multipliers for generators with 64 to 256 bits of state. Along the way, we correct some errors in the literature. In the end, we propose MWC192X, a 64-bit generator with 192 bits of state that passes all tests we are aware of, and emits an output in half a nanosecond.

title: Global Security Blind Spots: Translation as a Safety Bypass in Low-Resource Languages
summary: Large language models are deployed globally, yet safety alignment and evaluation remain concentrated in English: harmful requests refused in English can elicit unsafe completions when translated into low-resource languages. We evaluate ten widely deployed LLMs across 79 languages (English plus 78 low-resource) under a translation-bypass threat model, using a metric conditioned on English safety, which separates translation bypass from unsafety already present in English. English safety does not transfer reliably: conditioned on safe English completions, mean bypass rates range from 21.9% to 44.4%. Bypass risk concentrates in a subset of language families, a pattern broadly shared across models. The shared ordering is confounded with translation degeneracy, but its variation across models is significant and survives every control we apply. We also show that per-model bypass rates do not identify a stable ranking: nine of ten models change rank across three conditioning schemes that estimate the same quantity, with no change to any underlying response.

title: A Hybrid Information Flow Analysis Framework for Android Hybrid Apps
summary: The WebView interface in Android (hybrid) applications enables the native side (e.g., Java) to exchange data with the Web (e.g., JavaScript). This creates cross-language information flow channels that existing single-language analyzers cannot analyze. Existing hybrid app analyses address only part of the problem: some build bridge-aware call graphs but provide limited information-flow analysis, some rely on coarse assumptions, and some focus only on web vulnerabilities. We present MifDroid, a static-analysis- guided dynamic-analysis framework with a lifecycle-aware per-WebView call graph, a bridge-aware type-and-effect system, and a modular JavaScript analysis engine. We evaluated MifDroid on 338 apps from the F-Droid repository (out of 4,126 total) that use addJavascriptInterface, enabling active communication between Java and JavaScript. Our guided dynamic phase adds 662 entries to the 444 produced by static analysis, raising the resolution rate from 36.5% to 74.5%, produces the resolved bridge-related entries for 115 apps that static analysis leaves empty. MifDroid reported 14 vulnerable cross-language information flows, five of which have been accepted and fixed by the maintainers.

title: Guided Diffusion for Trustworthy Synthetic Text Generation
summary: The rapid evolution of Large Language Models is fueled by massive datasets, yet this reliance poses severe privacy risks, as models can inadvertently memorize and even directly output sensitive training data. Synthetic text generation offers a promising solution to this challenge; however, existing methods struggle to reconcile rigorous privacy guarantees with high data utility. In this paper, we propose a new paradigm for private synthetic text generation: Guided Diffusion. Leveraging the unique steerability of Diffusion Language Models, we introduce novel sampling and re-masking procedures that actively guide the iterative denoising steps. These mechanisms steer the generative process to reconstruct fluent text that adheres to a target semantic distribution. We demonstrate that our framework is naturally compatible with Differential Privacy (DP): once the semantic embeddings of the private corpus are protected, the DP guarantee carries over to the generated text by post-processing. Empirically, we show that our approach generates high-quality synthetic text with precise semantic alignment. Furthermore, we validate its effectiveness in DP synthetic text generation: across two datasets and two diffusion backbones, it outperforms Private Evolution and DP-SGD-based fine-tuning in distributional fidelity and downstream utility, while generating significantly faster than Private Evolution. We further extend the framework to Data-Specific Indistinguishability (DSI), which adds a formal certificate against data poisoning and memorization at a small utility cost.

title: When Models Know but Can't Linearly Say: Relational Encoding Limits Linear Vulnerability Classification in Code LLMs
summary: Large language models can detect vulnerable code, yet the form of vulnerability encoding in their representations remains unclear. We analyze 8 code models spanning 6.7B-15B parameters on C programs using three datasets (DELTASECOMMITS, SVEN, and PRECISE-BUGS), comparing two diagnostic tasks on the same representations: identifying what patterns the code instantiates, and determining whether it is vulnerable. Models encode the first with high fidelity. Under the studied paired C-code datasets and linear-probing setup, vulnerability information is more accessible as a paired relational signal-whether code A is riskier than code B-than as a globally separable categorical label. This structural difference has implications for classification: the model reliably ranks which code is riskier but standard classifiers on isolated samples achieve limited accuracy because vulnerable and secure samples form overlapping distributions in representation space.

title: When Pebbles Are Not Atomic: A Polynomial Separation Between Pure and Entangled Pebbling
summary:
Graph pebbling is the model in which the memory cost of memory-hard functions and proofs of space is measured, and pebbling lower bounds are the main way to argue that such constructions are secure. It has long seemed that the model is faithful to reality. It is known that it is not exact: an adversary who stores encoded information instead of whole values can do better, but so far only by small factors: a factor of 1.5 in the work that introduced entangled pebbling (Alwen, Chen, Kamath, Kolmogorov, Pietrzak and Tessaro) and, recently, a factor of about log n/log log n (de Rezende, Engström and Reyzin). One could still hope that pebbling is right up to such small factors.
  In pure pebbling, memory consists of whole labels; entangled pebbling also allows encoded state, such as XORs of labels. We show that the two models can differ polynomially. We study the setting in which proofs of space and data-dependent memory-hard functions are used: a state is prepared in advance, a random challenge has to be answered from it, and memory is paid for as long as it is held. Our graphs are explicit and have indegree two, and on them a pure adversary can do no better, up to a constant factor, than storing every possible answer in advance. Still, an adversary who keeps XORs instead of labels pays polynomially less. This ends the hope that pure pebbling is a faithful model of memory up to small factors.
  The heart of the paper is a simple combinatorial game, together with a special class of graphs found by Alon, Moitra and Sudakov.

title: AutoRedClaw: Automated Red-Teaming for Claw-Style Agents
summary: Agent systems are shifting from task-scoped tool-use agents to persistent, personalized assistants such as OpenClaw. These claw-style agents maintain configuration files (e.g., AGENTS.md), long-term memory, and reusable skills. Once poisoned, this persistent state is repeatedly reloaded into the agent's context, creating persistent threats across tasks and sessions. Existing security evaluation systems struggle to evaluate these complex claw-style systems since they rely heavily on manually constructed test cases and environments, which limits their scale and coverage; in addition, these manually designed cases quickly become outdated as agents evolve, and their evaluation settings leave a gap with how claw-style agents are deployed in practice. To address this, we introduce AutoRedClaw, an automated red-teaming framework that generates end-to-end attacks together with the environments needed to execute them. AutoRedClaw combines a strict quality-checking protocol with execution-based validation to ensure the correctness, realism, and effectiveness of generated samples, and adopts task-driven environment construction to keep costs low. To achieve broad coverage, it organizes generation along risk categories, attack strategies, attack stages, and attack surfaces, and uses experience-guided exploration to steer generation toward under-explored regions. AutoRedClaw achieves an effective attack rate above 30% at less than $0.10 per successful sample. From its outputs, we construct RedClaw-Bench, a 330-case benchmark that yields substantially higher attack success rates (ASRs) than AgentDojo, AgentDyn, and DTap. Across seven harnesses and four frontier models, most agent systems exceed 50% ASR, showing that our red-teaming pipeline provides a strong evaluation signal even for the most advanced agent systems. Our code and benchmark are released at https://github.com/SaFo-Lab/AutoRedClaw.

title: Profile-DP: Differential Privacy for User-Controlled Profile Release in Personalized LLM Inference
summary: Personalized large language models (LLMs) increasingly rely on profile-conditioned inference, pairing public requests with rich, user-specific facts. This paradigm exposes the user profile itself, together with the user's explicit sharing preferences. We introduce Profile-DP, a policy-aware local differential privacy framework designed specifically for user-profile release in personalized LLM inference. Profile-DP provably bounds the release of user-withheld facts while treating public instructions, profile schemas, and authorized facts as public side information. By generating a privatized profile that composes with the public instruction prior to answer generation, our framework decouples formal privacy guarantees from downstream model behavior. We develop two finite-domain mechanisms satisfying Profile-DP: DP-SLOT independently perturbs protected attributes, while DP-BLOCK uses public semantic decisions to coordinate their release and jointly sample related attributes. A positive, public compatibility prior connects these attributes while preserving a profile-level privacy bound. On PEEP, DP-BLOCK leads the utility composite among DP methods at all 13 structured budgets and is closest to the ideal privacy--utility point in 18 of 26 format--budget settings under our composite weighting. Direct measurements reveal complementary strengths: DP-BLOCK discloses less, while DP-SLOT retains more authorized facts. These results make policy-aware profile release a practical basis for studying privacy and personalization.

title: You Are the Trigger: Speaker-Activated Backdoors
summary: Speech models are increasingly used as an interface to AI systems, from transcription tools to voice agents. Existing audio backdoors require an attacker to introduce triggers at inference time. We study a different threat model in which the attacker compromises the model during fine-tuning but has no access to the victim's inference-time inputs. We introduce the Speaker-Activated Backdoor (SAB) setting, in which a target speaker's natural voice serves as the trigger. We develop a two-phase fine-tuning method that first makes speaker identity more accessible and then binds the target speaker to an attacker-chosen payload. Compared with a one-phase baseline with the same training budget, the two-phase method substantially improves selectivity and clean performance, and is especially important for content-dependent attacks. SAB achieves 90.2% and 97.0% backdoor success on Whisper-medium and Parakeet, with false-positive rates of 1.7% and 0%, respectively using as little as two minutes of real audio from the target speaker. We further demonstrate content-dependent semantic rewriting and downstream tool-use attacks, where malicious instructions are inserted into 96.9% of target-speaker transcripts. When these transcripts are passed to frontier LLM agents, GPT-4o and Claude (Opus, Sonnet, and Haiku), the injected instruction drives the agent to carry out the harmful action in up to 87.5% of cases. The attack generalizes to held-out recordings, multiple target speakers, and common acoustic degradations. These results establish speaker identity as a practical backdoor trigger that requires no inference-time attacker access and is invisible at the transcript layer.

title: A Combined Streaming FPGA Architecture for Client-Side CKKS Encoding and Encryption
summary: Homomorphic encryption allows a computing service to process encrypted data, but the client must first encode and encrypt its inputs. Sharing hardware between floating-point encoding and modular encryption reduces area but requires those transform roles to execute at different times. We present a streaming FPGA architecture for CKKS encoding and encryption that computes the shared floating-point encoding transform once and performs the integer transforms for six residue moduli in parallel. Dedicated transform pipelines exchange intermediate results on chip rather than through off-chip memory. DSP Builder generates the transform RTL, and Altera HLS IP Gen compiler compiles the surrounding SYCL pipeline into IP integrated with DMA and control logic in an accelerator functional unit. At polynomial degree N = 8192, the Altera Agilex 7 implementation delivers 5,143 complete ciphertexts per second at 471 MHz. One SEAL-Embedded CPU worker on the same workstation delivers 113 ciphertexts per second for real-valued inputs using all 4,096 slots. Measurements cover prepared-input computation through complete ciphertext construction, including FPGA submission and output delivery.

title: Model Exposure on One Device Endangers Others: Rethinking Edge Neural Network Security across Devices
summary: Neural networks (NNs) are increasingly deployed on edge devices such as mobile and IoT platforms, offering low latency and improved privacy compared to cloud-based deployment. However, on-device models embedded in mobile applications can be unpacked and exposed to adversaries, enabling cross-node attacks in centrally distributed ecosystems, where adversarial examples crafted on one compromised device transfer effectively to other nodes sharing the same models. To address this threat, we propose VeilNN, a defense framework that reduces adversarial transferability across on-device models via model obfuscation. The core idea of VeilNN is to introduce controlled model diversity while preserving original task functionality. Specifically, VeilNN applies stealthy and irreversible obfuscation at both the architectural and parameter levels through network cell obfuscation and layer assembling, and is applicable to diverse NN architectures, including MLPs, CNNs, and Vision Transformers. Extensive experiments demonstrate that VeilNN effectively defends against cross-node attacks, achieving an average defense success of 49.19% and up to 81.19% across four adversarial attack types, with more than 33.16% improvement over existing defenses.

title: Mind Your Boundaries: Boundary-Aware Model Obfuscation against Cross-node Attack
summary: With the advancement of powerful AI chips, on-device machine learning is gaining traction for its low latency and privacy protection. However, when edge devices are compromised, attackers can obtain white-box access to the deployed models by reversing the apps directly to obtain the knowledge of peer devices, which is known as Cross-Node Attacks, like performing efficient adversarial attacks. Most existing defenses target known vulnerabilities, yet white-box access still enables attackers to uncover more unknown weaknesses. This creates a critical risk for edge-device deployments, where one compromised device can endanger all models distributed from the same source. Motivated by findings that the model robustness is primarily influenced by the curvature of the decision boundary, we investigate how model parameters shape its curvature. In this paper, we propose a novel method, BMO, that obfuscates model parameters to diversify the decision boundary further resisting cross-node attack while preserving its benign accuracy. Specifically, we explore decomposing model parameters into boundary-position and boundary-curvature components based on null-space constraints, then models with differentiated decision boundaries are instantiated by injecting noise into the boundary-curvature component. Across all four major types of adversarial attacks with four widely-deployed on-device models, BMO achieves an average success rate of 68.68% in defense, far exceeding the most competitive baseline, which attains only 22.32% in defending against cross-node attacks. Moreover, BMO achieves comparable performance in benign accuracy compared with baselines.

title: Energy Consumption of Post-Quantum Cryptography on Constrained and General-Purpose Architectures
summary: With Q-day approaching, the transition to post-quantum cryptography (PQC) has begun, with governments across the US, UK and EU mandating migration to quantum-resistant standards. This paper benchmarks the three NIST-standardised PQC algorithms - FIPS 203 (ML-KEM), FIPS 204 (ML-DSA) and FIPS 205 (SLH-DSA) - across key generation, signing and verification operations, measuring both computational performance and energy consumption on a range of constrained IoT-class devices, from the 32-bit Raspberry Pi 1 and Zero to the 64-bit Raspberry Pi 4, as well as commodity laptop hardware. Using the FNIRSI FNB58 USB power meter and OpenSSL~3.5, results show that ML-KEM and ML-DSA achieve energy and speed efficiency comparable to classical elliptic-curve cryptography across all tested architectures. However, SLH-DSA signing is inadvisable on constrained hardware: energy costs for SLH-DSA signing on 32-bit devices were up to 243\% higher than on equivalent 64-bit hardware, making it impractical for resource-limited IoT deployments. These findings have direct implications for IoT security practitioners planning PQC migration.

title: ECHO: Revealing Review-to-Submission Linkage in Anonymous Peer Review
summary: Anonymous peer review protects reviewers from retaliation, yet reviewer anonymity may also be weakened by artifacts released through the review process itself. This risk is growing as many venues require submitting authors to review, creating substantial overlap between authors and reviewers within the same review cycle. We identify review-to-submission linkage, where an anonymous review can be associated with the reviewer's own submission, substantially shrinking the reviewer anonymity set. To assess whether this linkage is practically exploitable, we develop ECHO, which combines technical-expertise and writing-style signals across reviews, papers, and rebuttals, and evaluate it on R2S-Bench, a ground-truth benchmark we construct. ECHO correctly identifies the reviewer's own submission in Top-1 for 34.6% of reviews, in the Top-5 for 54.0%, and in the Top-10 for 63.4%, compared with 0.5%, 2.6%, and 5.3% under random ranking, from the candidate submissions. With a stronger Stage-2 reranker, ECHO further reaches 56.4% Top-1 and 66.4% Top-10. These results demonstrate that review-to-submission linkage is feasible using only routinely released peer-review artifacts. Code and benchmark are available at https://github.com/kaimu11111/ECHO-Revealing-Review-to-Submission-Linkage-in-Anonymous-Peer-Review.

title: Accountable partial understanding: securing the epistemic attack surface of agentic systems
summary: Attackers profit from what defenders do not understand. Software security has treated the gap between system behavior and human comprehension as a condition to narrow through analysis and assurance, booking the remainder as accepted risk. Agentic AI systems change that gap: when software reads, writes, explains, and authorizes security-relevant behavior, partial understanding moves faster, grows more opaque, and couples to delegated authority. This paper characterizes the resulting epistemic attack surface and presents a taxonomy of four interacting attack categories, which target the interpretation of intent, the production and consumption of evidence, the scope of delegated authority, and the comprehension of human supervisors. It then defines accountable partial understanding (APU) and specifies six necessary conditions: bounded scope with explicit assumptions, inspectable evidence, assigned responsibility, visible residual unknowns, actionability, and temporal maintenance. It explains why delegating interpretation to software agents differs from distributing knowledge among people and distinguishes APU from risk acceptance, explainable AI, assurance cases, formal verification, and human-in-the-loop oversight. From the conditions, the paper derives five design principles: bounded delegation, decoupled evidence, assumption tracking with invalidation, role-specific accountability views, and intervention-preserving design with residual unknown registers. It introduces two measurable probe dimensions, evidence linkage and invalidation latency, for testing whether accountability mechanisms hold under change and adversarial pressure. Three running examples (an AI coding agent, an autonomous cyber-defense agent, and an AI-mediated insulin delivery update) ground the analysis. Security without full understanding is already here; the task is to make it accountable.

title: Game of Phones: Harnessing Game Theory and LLMs in 'Bot Wars' to Counteract Phone Scams
summary: Phone scams impose substantial and growing costs on individuals and financial systems worldwide, yet existing countermeasures impose no resource cost on perpetrators. Strategic scam-baiting, in which automated agents engage scammers to deplete their operational capacity, offers a proactive alternative but requires dynamic strategy adaptation that static systems cannot provide. We introduce a game-theoretic framework enabling LLMs to learn effective counter-strategies through in-context experience without fine-tuning. The framework models scammer-baiter interactions as a two-player game with empirically grounded strategies and utility functions, using Nash equilibrium as a formal benchmark for evaluating learned behaviour. Across 300 simulated dialogues and three LLM architectures, adaptive strategy selection achieves 28.9-79.7% closer alignment to Nash equilibrium than non-adaptive baselines. The code and an annotated dataset of 300 dialogues with turn-level strategy labels and utility scores are released at https://github.com/nardinebasta/GameofPhones_/ .

title: Proof-of-Machine-Learning-Inference: Mining Knowledge, Not Hashes
summary: Bitcoin-style Proof-of-Work (PoW) secures permissionless blockchains but spends substantial computation on hash puzzles which have no utility other than extending the chain. At the same time, we have seen that the rise of generative AI has created significant demand for computational resources that are unfortunately available only to a few players. We propose a solution that solves both problems at the same time. In particular, we present Proof-of-ML-Inference (PoML), a consensus protocol in which miners perform user-requested machine-learning inference as part of their consensus algorithm. We identify exactly what computational assumptions are needed for ML inference to safely replace hash work, formalize those assumptions, and give evidence that LLMs and diffusion models satisfy them. We then formally analyse the security of our protocol by reducing the security of our protocol to the security of the Bitcoin Backbone model. Finally, we empirically evaluate block-time stability, showing that, in a simulated environment, PoML maintains a block production rate close to its calibrated block-time target.

title: BrushOff: Stroke-Based Re-rendering as a Watermark Removal Attack on Painting
summary: Invisible watermarks are used to mark who owns a painting. We show that a simple attack removes the most robust one we test. The attack redraws the watermarked painting with brush strokes, using a pretrained stroke-based renderer. We call this attack BrushOff. It needs no training, no knowledge of the watermark, and no generative model. We test four watermarks on 500 paintings from five styles. VINE, a recent watermark built to survive image editing, survives all 14 conventional distortions we test, with at least 97.8% detection. Repainting lowers its detection to 1.8%, while the output keeps a no-reference quality score close to that of the clean paintings. Diffusion regeneration can also remove VINE, but at the same removal level it moves the image twice as far from the painting in DreamSim distance, and it changes what the painting shows. Because the renderer draws a countable number of strokes, we can control the attack strength step by step. Finally, we test what kind of signal survives. A simple probe that stores bits in the relative brightness of neighboring regions survives repainting, while a probe that uses absolute brightness does not. The same probe fails under diffusion regeneration, while VINE fails under repainting. Robustness to these two attacks is therefore a separate property, and benchmarks should test both.

title: DM-RSA-OAEP: Formal Treatment of a Dual-Modulus Fault-Detection Countermeasure Based on Physical Diversity
summary: We revisit DM-RSA, an RSA variant that uses two independent moduli, whose original version was broken by Håstad's attack and contained an incorrect compromise-tolerance claim. We give a formal treatment of its repaired variant, DM-RSA-OAEP: (i) a complete IND-CCA2 security proof in the random-oracle model via a two-step hybrid argument, upper-bounding the security of the scheme by that of the weaker underlying RSA-OAEP instance, with an explicit simulation loss; (ii) a fault-detection theorem in an explicit adversary model that covers computation, key, and verification faults, including safe-error attacks, under a clearly stated physical-diversity assumption; (iii) an explicit analysis of why the countermeasure degrades to uselessness when the diversity assumption is violated (common-mode faults on a single chip). We position the scheme against the countermeasure landscape and against the broken dual-modulus literature. The contribution is deliberately framed as a fault countermeasure with a provable detection guarantee, not as a computationally stronger RSA. We conclude with a concrete instantiation and a detailed measurement protocol.

title: Beyond Attack Success Rate: Cost-Aware Metric for Evaluating Iterative LLM Jailbreaks
summary: Attack success rate (ASR) evaluates jailbreaks against large language models without accounting for repeated calls to the victim model. Yet each additional call gives the deployed system another opportunity to detect the attack and intervene. We introduce $\mathrm{ASR}_{\mathrm{STEP}}$, which penalizes additional victim-model calls while retaining binary success judgments. Our evaluation considers GCG, PAIR with a step budget, and a single-step PAP baseline on JailBreakBench across three model families. GCG's scores decrease by 7.0-8.7 percentage points after discounting, while PAP's remain unchanged. While for PAIR attack, we see a wider discounting range between 3.4-12 percentage points, showing that the "step" quantity differs per iterative strategy. Reporting both metrics makes the discount due to repeated victim-model interaction explicit. Code is available here: https://github.com/SuELS-Group/beyond_asr.

title: BR-MoE: Budgeted Semantic Release for Privacy-Preserving Traffic Analytics
summary: Traffic cameras support useful analysis, but their outputs can reveal private information. Replacing images with text reduces direct visual exposure. It does not place a formal bound on disclosure. The published reinforcement learning and mixture-of-experts framework refines scene descriptions through relevance, coverage, and brevity rewards. It does not account for repeated releases under a fixed privacy budget. This paper proposes budgeted semantic release as an extension of that framework. Four scene experts first process isolated video chunks. Their outputs are mapped to a fixed, bounded semantic schema. A reinforcement learning controller selects which expert summaries to release and how much privacy budget to spend. The controller uses public task requests and previous private releases. A separate privacy filter enforces the total budget. Calibrated noise is added before the summaries are converted to text. Under explicit chunk isolation and bounded-event assumptions, the complete release transcript satisfies an event-level differential privacy bound. The design also supports reuse of previous summaries without new disclosure. An evaluation protocol covers traffic utility, privacy attacks, release freshness, and computational cost. Illustrative tables show the intended reporting format. They do not establish empirical gains. The proposed contribution is a task-aware release interface with auditable privacy accounting for repeated traffic descriptions.

title: Connection Escrow: Holding AI-Agent Pod Egress in the Kernel Until an Isolated Verifier Rules
summary: AI agents in containers act by opening network connections, and the text that drives them can be hostile. Controls placed between the agent and its tools are bypassed by a child process or a direct socket, and their approval is not tied to the connection the kernel later opens. We present connection escrow: every outbound TCP connection from a supervised pod is parked inside the kernel's connect() path, before any packet exists, by a 98-instruction eBPF program on the pod's cgroup. A node interceptor attributes the held socket to its kernel socket cookie, process, executable digest, cgroup and pod identity, parks the first bytes the agent writes, and asks a verifier in a separate container with its own key. The connection is released only on a signed verdict naming that one socket cookie and destination, unexpired and unused; no verdict by the deadline resets it, and a late approval is refused. The agent is unmodified. A 36-check adversarial suite with real cgroups passes on the eBPF hold point (33 of the checks also apply, and pass, on an iptables hold point): refused connections never reach the destination; forged, rebound, replayed, expired and late verdicts are refused; the agent's attempt to reach the verifier is itself escrowed; child-process and renamed-binary bypasses fail; UDP is pinned to the resolver. On a Kubernetes cluster, unmodified pods are held per connection and attributed to their SPIFFE identity, a raw socket that bypasses a sidecar proxy is held, and 600 connections from six pods are gated. The hold adds 4.5 ms median per released connection, of which 24 us is policy. Finally, we gate on request content without terminating TLS: an eBPF uprobe reads the plaintext at the agent's TLS-library boundary (shared OpenSSL, static OpenSSL, Go crypto/tls), a model scores it, and the connection is held on that verdict while TLS stays end-to-end and the enforcer holds no key.

title: Mal-AAEGAN: Adversarial Autoencoder with Double-Critic WGAN-GP for Malware Generation
summary: Machine-learning (ML) malware detectors are known to be vulnerable to adversarial samples. Generative adversarial networks (GANs) such as MalGAN, Mal-LSGAN, and our previous Mal-D2GAN can craft adversarial malware to probe and harden these detectors, yet they operate directly on a high-dimensional, discrete binary feature space, which leads to unstable training, vanishing gradients, and adversarial samples of limited diversity. To address these problems we propose Mal-AAEGAN. First, an adversarial autoencoder (AAE) learns a low-dimensional, regularized and continuous latent representation of the $M$-dimensional binary API feature vector, and the generator performs an additive perturbation in this latent space rather than in the raw binary space. Second, training follows the Wasserstein GAN with gradient penalty (WGAN-GP) scheme using two critics: a mimic-black-box critic that inherits the role of the substitute detector and a naive critic that inherits the role of the additional detector. A decode-binarize-OR pipeline guarantees that the original API calls of the malware are preserved. The model is evaluated on two malware datasets of different input dimensionality ($M\in\{139,215\}$) against eight common ML detectors and compared, under an identical protocol, with MalGAN, Mal-LSGAN and Mal-D2GAN. Mal-AAEGAN trains stably in the continuous latent space and attains an evasion rate on par with or higher than these binary-space baselines across both datasets, while its generator stays responsive to the noise input rather than reducing to a single fixed perturbation per malware.

title: Differential privacy with adjustable preservation of multivariate relationships
summary: This paper derives an exact attenuation formula for multivariate cross-moments under differential privacy achieved through randomized response. From a proposed alternative formulation of randomization matrices compliant with differential privacy guarantees we show that, under attribute-level randomization and where the randomization of the whole distribution is characterized by Kronecker products, any cross-moment of the anonymized dataset involving distinct attributes is equal to the original cross-moment multiplied by attenuation parameters, themselves determined by the part of the overall privacy budget allocated to each attribute. This characterization enables explicit and transparent controls of multivariate relationships preservations in differential privacy through privacy budget allocation. A simple numerical illustration demonstrates that identical total budgets can yield substantially different covariance-preservation profiles. The results also make the multiplicative loss of higher-order interactions explicit and thus can support mechanism design guided by analytical priorities.

title: Exact Compilation and Resource Laws for Hidden Integer Feedback
summary: Hidden randomized rounding couples the privacy loss of successive integer releases. We study a rational-feedback mechanism under predictable signed-unit participation and full observation of every physical output. A preparation's lifetime connects three results. First, preserving complete carries until an observed echo synchronizes the worlds gives exact finite-law point compilation, with support-width exponent $3C-2$ at every fixed budget $C\ge2$. Second, releasing commitments earlier gives a monotone hierarchy whose exact endpoint, strict gaps and numerical brackets quantify calibration loss. At one fixed discrete Gaussian, a loss allowance of 0.09 requires all four commitments. Third, legal regeneration yields an unrestricted KL rate with a square-root testing remainder and a complete asymptotic frontier under joint physical-time and participation constraints. At fixed rational parameters, finite-window occupation programs approximate that frontier to error $2^{-b}$ in polynomial bit time in $b$. Verified countable-transcript semantics and independently checked finite certificates support these analyses. A matched static workload illustrates the resulting design tradeoff: a structured finite integer matrix improves error and fresh randomness, while the scalar feedback instance retains fewer noise-state and source-table bits.

title: Reliable Estimation of Differential Privacy under Selection Bias
summary: Statistical privacy audits are essential for verifying the theoretical privacy guarantees of differentially private (DP) mechanisms. Auditors typically use Membership Inference Attacks (MIAs) to estimate a lower bound on the true privacy leakage of DP mechanisms at a specified confidence level, which should not exceed the theoretical privacy upper bound guaranteed by DP. However, we found that many auditing implementations in prior work introduce a selection bias when running MIAs, which leads to statistically invalid and overestimated lower bounds. Because most audits are not tight, this bias has thus far gone unnoticed: the estimated lower bounds remained well below the theoretical upper bounds. Nevertheless, accurately evaluating this lower bound is critical, as a flawed statistical assessment could lead to false alarms on correct mechanisms or an incorrect evaluation of the guarantee's tightness. This work employs tools from the statistical literature to correct this bias. We present an overview of the different correction methods and assess their respective advantages. Furthermore, we perform a comprehensive re-analysis of results returned by prior audit implementations and show that without statistical correction, these audits violate the theoretical upper bounds up to four times more often than their claimed confidence level implies. With correction applied, the resulting lower bounds are statistically valid, and violations occur at no more than the nominal rate.

title: Fake News, Real Crashes: Information Injection Attacks on LLM Financial Trading Agents
summary: Large language model (LLM) agents now trade real capital using news as evidence, yet they cannot reliably tell fabricated headlines from real news. Because they read the same feeds under near-identical policies, a single fabricated post can push them into the same trade at the same moment. We present a systematic attack benchmark for information injection against LLM trading agents. Unlike prompt injection, which targets the model's instructions, information injection targets the evidence the agent trusts. The benchmark spans five injection vectors and seven event categories, evaluated over ~10,000 decisions on 15 U.S. stocks. Five findings emerge. (i) Prompt injection achieves 14% attack success rate (ASR), but fabricated news reaches 62% and two 30-word templates reach 100% on all 15 stocks, inverting the usual LLM-security intuition. (ii) For fact-poisoning templates, surface form matters more than content, since removing credibility cues such as a named source or a "BREAKING" tag drops ASR from 100% to 0% while the fake claim remains identical. (iii) Success depends on the agent's state, with a fake indicator panel scoring 91% against an agent about to hold but 12% against one about to buy. (iv) Attacks generalize across model vendors and remain effective when blended, unlabeled, into real news feeds. (v) Most attacks evade standard defenses, since model scaling stops shallow vectors but not fact poisoning, peer debate fails, and only hierarchical aggregation reduces ASR.

title: Temporal Dynamics and Security Assessment of SRT Protocol: A 96-Day Longitudinal Analysis of Production Streaming Infrastructure
summary: This study presents a 96-day longitudinal analysis of Secure Reliable Transport (SRT) protocol behavior in a production streaming environment between Iraq and Turkey, examining 262,672 transport metric samples and 5,033,104 system resource measurements collected between October 2025 and January 2026. The research addresses temporal patterns, system-resource relationships, attack vulnerability, and anomaly detection. Results reveal significant temporal variation: Negative Acknowledgment exhibits 7.6-fold hourly variation and 11.5-fold daily variation (p < 0.001), though with small effect sizes (eta^2 < 0.04), indicating that temporal period explains less than 4 percent of total variance. Central Processing Unit (CPU) utilization emerges as the strongest system-level correlate of transport variation (r = 0.617 with NAK rate). Controlled User Datagram Protocol (UDP) flood experiments at 500 packets per second cause CPU increases of 176 to 806 percent, while SRT transport metrics change by only plus or minus 13 percent demonstrating protocol resilience through the Automatic Repeat Request mechanism. An unexpected anomaly reaching 97.7 percent CPU enabled signature-based differentiation between attack types. A Z-score anomaly detection method outperforms fixed thresholds, detecting all 7 security events. This study contributes the longest temporal characterization of SRT metrics reported to date, the first system-SRT correlation analysis, and the first controlled security assessment of SRT infrastructure. These findings provide actionable guidance for capacity planning, security hardening, and multi-metric monitoring of production SRT deployments.

title: Fortress: Fork Resistant Transparency logs Relying on Social graph Structure
summary:
Transparency systems -- such as Key Transparency (KT), Certificate Transparency, and binary transparency -- require that all honest participants see the same view of an untrusted server's directory, or, failing that, that the misbehaviour is publicly detected. Every existing design closes this gap with an external trust anchor: a publicly available bulletin board (BB), a blockchain, or an out-of-band (OOB) gossip network among auditors.
  We observe that transparency systems already have a built-in resource that has so far been overlooked: the social graph induced by the users themselves. We ask whether it can replace the bulletin board or the external gossip channel entirely, and answer in the affirmative (if occasional out-of-band interactions are allowed).
  We formalise a new primitive, Social-Graph based Forking-Resilient Transparency (sg-FORT), which captures the security guarantees of a BB-free transparency system and we construct Fortress Fork Resistant Transparency logs Relying on Social graph Structure, to our knowledge the first such protocol. In every epoch either all users output the same post, or at least one honest user produces a publicly verifiable Proof of Misbehaviour. Our guarantees hold against an arbitrary malicious server, including a snapshot adversary that may compromise a user and learn its secret state, as long as the server does not compromise close users. In honest executions, OOB interactions occur only when a user resets their secrets, so the total OOB cost approaches the natural lower bound of one call per reset -- dramatically below the full-gossip alternative. We prove security under standard cryptographic assumptions on signatures and dictionary commitment. Under simplifying assumptions (synchronous epochs, always-online users), we view this as a first feasibility result that opens up the design space of social-graph-based transparency systems.

title: Q-MALDetect: Quantum Image-Based Malware Detection and Adversarial Robustness Analysis
summary: Quantum machine-learning (QML) models are increasingly considered for security applications, yet their adversarial robustness in malware analysis remains insufficiently understood. This paper presents Q-MALDetect, a hybrid convolutional and variational-quantum detector for byte-image representations of x86-64 Executable and Linkable Format (ELF) binaries, and evaluates it under feature-space and a range of Grad-CAM-guided, executable-aware evasion attacks. The model achieves 97.2% training accuracy, but its robustness deteriorates as attack strength increases, with the strongest evaluated feature-space attack reaching a 78.7% attack success rate (ASR). Among executable-aware attacks, Grad-CAM-guided no-operation (NOP) insertion produces the highest conditional ASR of 32.9%. Dynamic adversarial training is the most effective evaluated defense, reducing feature-space ASR to as low as 5.0%, executable-aware ASR to 7.7%, and the sequential-attack ASR to 34.0%. In contrast, convolutional-autoencoder preprocessing increases executable-aware ASR to 39.7%, coinciding with a rise in Grad-CAM attribution mass within the mutable .text region from 35.2% to 45.7%. Ablation results reveal no monotonic relationship between qubit count and robustness, while the encoding interface modifies the learned attack surface without neutralizing the strongest attack. These findings demonstrate that the effectiveness of attacks and defenses depends strongly on the perturbation constraints and evaluation conditions. Reliable deployment of QML malware detectors therefore requires assessment against both feature-space and executable-aware attacks rather than reliance on clean accuracy or generic denoising alone.

title: Signature Knowledge Shielding: Protecting Antivirus Detection Knowledge through Robust Embedding Matching
summary: Antivirus (AV) signatures encode valuable detection knowledge accumulated through expert analysis, yet repeated black-box queries can expose this knowledge for unauthorized reuse and targeted evasion. We propose Signature Knowledge Shielding (SKS), a design paradigm that protects existing AV rules, termed Protected Signatures (PS), through auxiliary Shielding Signatures (SS). SKS uses AV-supervised importance ranking to discover candidate byte blocks, filters and selects them through negative-sample calibration, and combines SS matches with original AV verdicts through logical OR. SS matching introduces additional positive responses and verdict changes during probing, making detection feedback less directly attributable to PS and increasing the difficulty of localizing signature-related content, while preserving original positive verdicts. Within SKS, we integrate five individually tuned non-learning matching methods and further propose Robust Embedding Matching (REM), a lightweight learned matcher trained with random context and byte perturbations. REM provides stronger and more consistent protection against content modifications and scanning-alignment changes. We develop and open-source a ClamAV-based prototype and evaluate it against five probing methods. With an observed additional test false-positive rate below 0.1%, REM raises the mean query count of state-of-the-art probing to as much as 282.57 times the unprotected baseline, while introducing only 0.67% GPU scanning overhead. These results demonstrate that SKS can substantially increase signature-extraction costs with limited impact on detection utility and scanning efficiency.

title: PhantomTac: Hijacking Robotic Tactile Systems with Deploy-and-forget Tags
